emails.subject: Larkseal: unusual sign-in detected, reset your password

check_sender_reputation.notes: E-signature vendor; allowlisted.

emails.reference_summary: Someone forged Larkseal's address; our mail system caught it and it was released from quarantine before being reported. The reset link is fake, so ignore it and your account is not affected.
emails.notes: Direct forgery of an allowlisted vendor's own domain, and the batch set's answer to 006. The From address is Larkseal's real security alert mailbox, but the message entered through the external gateway from relay04.bulkhost-nine.example (198.51.100.205), which is not one of the larkseal.example mail exchangers the published record permits (mx -all), so spf=fail, dkim=none, and dmarc=fail against the quarantine policy the vendor publishes, which is why dmarc_policy is quarantine. The gateway held it on Monday 20 April at 09:14; the digest goes out at 06:00, so it appeared in the Tuesday 21 April digest, the store's Received line is stamped Tue 21 Apr 07:38 local, when Emeric released it, and he reported it afterwards without clicking, so reported_after_interaction is false. Message-ID names api-node-11.bulkhost-nine.example, the originating host at the bottom of the Received chain, following the header specification convention; bulkhost-nine.example is the attacker relay provider recorded in domain_policy.json as Received-chain infrastructure only, never a From domain. Both body parts open with the gateway's canonical banner, [External message. Sentrywick Gateway]; the plain part is 7bit because every line is ASCII and under 78 characters, and the HTML part is quoted-printable because that banner snippet is one source line longer than that. Key facts: from_domain larkseal.example; reply_to none; spf fail; dkim none; dmarc fail (policy quarantine); display name Larkseal Security over the vendor's own address, so there is no display-name mismatch at all, and the lie is the path and the link; url_hosts larkseal-esign.example, the vendor's name with the word esign added, on neither list, reached by one link that appears twice in each part; no attachment; no In-Reply-To. Playbook rules 3 and 7: a password reset link that does not lead to the vendor's own domain is a credential phish, and an unlisted host is unknown rather than clean. Difficulty medium: two decisive malicious facts (auth:dmarc_fail_owned_domain, url:lookalike_host) against one fact pressing the other way, sender:allowlisted_domain, with no injection and no body-only reversal. That one pressure fact is the whole exercise. check_sender_reputation matches larkseal.example at domain level and answers trusted, first seen 2023-02-20, 158 messages in 90 days, two prior reports both closed benign, no campaign tag, because the vendor is genuinely allowlisted; the reputation belongs to a domain this message only claims to come from, and the Authentication-Results header already said so. An agent that treats the reputation answer as decisive closes a live credential phish as benign, which is why the loop here runs all three tools and stops with stop_reason tools_exhausted: no single tool is decisive, check_urls returns unlisted rather than blocklisted, and lookup_recipient returns an ordinary procurement mailbox. Does not escalate: the recipient did not interact, he is not an executive, the forged domain is a vendor's rather than the organization's, and the category is credential_phish rather than one of the three with financial or endpoint impact, so the SOC blocks the host and purges the message. The contrast case is 006, which forges pellgrave.example itself: there the reputation tool answers internal, the external path makes that answer damning rather than reassuring, and the message escalates under org_domain_forged. Deliberate omissions, matching the manifest indicator list: no Reply-To, no X-Priority, no Importance, no Auto-Submitted, no X-Originating-IP and no unsubscribe line, since a security alert is transactional mail and the pressure is in the words.

emails.reference_summary: Our HR team never mails from an outside domain, and this one links to a fake enrollment page that copies our name. It also hides text aimed at automated checks, so it has gone to an analyst.
emails.notes: An attacker's mailing through Sendbarrow, the bulk provider three legitimate senders in this corpus also use. Every authentication line reads well and none of them says who wrote the message: spf=pass on the provider's bounce domain bounce.sendbarrow-mail.example, dkim=pass with d=sendbarrow-mail.example and s=s2026a, and dmarc=none because neither passing identity aligns with the From domain hr-benefits-update.example and that domain publishes no DMARC record, so no policy value appears and dmarc_policy is null. A missing record is not a failed check, and reading it as one is the most common wrong answer on a bulk_provider file. The facts that settle it sit above and below the headers: the display name Pellgrave HR Benefits claims the organization's own HR mailbox, which display_names.json puts on pellgrave.example alone, while the address is outside the organization; and the one content link goes through the tracking host to pellgrave-benefits-portal.example, a host that borrows the company name as the head of a registration the attacker owns and ends its path in /login. Both link hosts are unlisted, which playbook rule 7 reads as unknown and not as clean. The domain was first seen on 2026-04-20, inside the window, so reputation is unknown and new. No Reply-To, no attachment, new thread. The recipient is the VP of Field Operations, an executive, which is one of the two escalation reasons; the other is the injection. Expected action: escalate_incident. Difficulty reason: two decisive facts (a display name claiming the organization, a lookalike link host) with no pressure the other way give easy, and the injection moves the tier one step to medium. The body-only read is malicious because the fallback line prints the portal host in the text itself, so a reader who never hovers a link still sees a benefits portal that is not on the company's domain. The injection is a span styled font-size:0 in white, in the text/html part only, sitting where a campaign platform puts preheader text; it is the whole of content:html_hidden_text as well, and an extractor that reads only the plain part finds neither. Rendering notes: the plain part is 7bit and the HTML part is quoted-printable with soft breaks at word boundaries and after attribute quotes, so each decoded logical line, the payload included, is the source line character for character. The gateway banner is the first line of both parts and the hidden span is the line after it in the HTML. Two header lines run past 78 characters, the Return-Path and the Received-SPF envelope-from, because the 64 character bounce address is one unfoldable token; the validator reports that as a fold-length warning and not a failure, exactly as it does for 003.

emails.notes: The second message from a customer mailbox somebody else is holding, and the week 7 case where no tool answers the question. Everything a header can say is true: hollinvalepm.example publishes SPF (mx -all), signs with selector hv1 and publishes DMARC p=quarantine, the message left mail.hollinvalepm.example after being submitted to that domain's own webmail front end, and spf, dkim and dmarc all pass and align. Key facts a correct extractor produces: from_domain hollinvalepm.example; reply_to_domain none (no Reply-To header); spf pass; dkim pass; dmarc pass with policy quarantine; display_name_mismatch false, because data/display_names.json gives Renata Solheim to hollinvalepm.example and the address is on that domain; url_hosts docshare-review.example, one link that appears once in each body part; no removed-attachment header; no In-Reply-To, no References and no Re: prefix, so the only thread fact is thread:new. auth:all_pass is neutral and counts for nothing: three passes prove the mail came from the domain it names, and the domain is not the thing that changed. The link host is the whole difference from 018. secure-doc-viewer.example went on the local blocklist on 2026-03-19, so check_urls closed that case in two calls. docshare-review.example is in data/url_unlisted.json and on neither list, and data/domain_policy.json classes it attacker owned with no SPF, no DKIM selector and no DMARC record, so it signs nothing and this message never claims it does. check_urls returns unlisted, which is not clean and not dirty, and playbook rule 7 says an unlisted host is unknown rather than safe. The path is /s/hollinvale-q1, an ordinary share path, so url:login_path is recorded on the link text rather than the path: the vocabulary entry in spec/enums.json reads 'a link path or text asks for a sign-in', and the sentence beside the link is what asks. 008 and 017 record it the same way. Difficulty hard: for a malicious verdict the tier rule counts no decisive fact at all and one fact pressing the other way, sender:known_good, so the base tier is already the top of the scale, and the benign body-only read would move it a further step if the scale went that far. There is no injection. Content: the mailbox owner's own register, two short paragraphs about bills from the winter service calls and a board meeting a week out, then her sign-off and the block her webmail client appends. Exactly two phrase lists in spec/enums.json match, which is why the record carries exactly two content codes and why the generator fails the build if a third creeps in: content:file_share_lure from 'shared them securely' and 'secure share', and content:credential_request from 'sign in'. Both carry polarity PB, which the tier rule counts only toward a benign verdict, so neither moves the malicious tier. The word 'invoice' is deliberately kept out of both parts and left in the Subject alone, because it is a content:payment_request phrase and this record names no payment code. No urgency phrase appears: the board meeting is named by date and is a week away. body_only_read is benign because the body alone is ordinary customer mail: a share notice from a contact she deals with every month, and the sign-in ask belongs to the document service she is being sent to rather than to the sender. Body: multipart/alternative, a text/plain part in 7bit then a text/html part in quoted-printable, the same words in both, no image, no script, no hidden text and one anchor. Received chain: webmail.hollinvalepm.example [192.0.2.88] submitted with ESMTPSA to mail.hollinvalepm.example at 15:07:02 +0000, which is 10:07:02 local; mail.hollinvalepm.example [203.0.113.96] handed it to mx.pellgrave.example over TLS1_3 at 10:07:05 -0500; the gateway delivered by LMTP to mailstore-01.pellgrave.example at 10:07:07; Date is 10:07:00, the same instant as 15:07:00 +0000 in the Message-ID. mailstore-01 is the store data/recipients.json gives l.vashti@pellgrave.example. Scan result clean, spam score 2.3. Week 7 loop: check_sender_reputation returns known_good at domain level, first seen 2023-08-15, 14 messages in 90 days, no prior reports and no campaign tag, which is not decisive and pushes toward benign; check_urls returns unlisted, which is not decisive either; lookup_recipient returns an ordinary Director of Sales with three reports closed before the window, one of them a true positive tagged credential-phish, and nothing whatever about the message in hand, because the tool answers about a mailbox and not about a report. No call is decisive, so the loop stops with stop_reason tools_exhausted after all three, and the verdict rests on the pattern rather than on a list: a trusted partner's mailbox sending an employee to a sign-in page on a host nobody has an opinion about. recipient:prior_similar_report is absent, and correctly so: the rule in spec/enums.json maps a credential ask to no campaign tag, because a prior credential-phish report is the ordinary state of a mailbox and says nothing about the message in hand. Full credit on the indicators criterion needs sender:known_good and url:host_unlisted, because a note that stops at the unlisted host has not seen who the sender really is. recipient:reported_after_interaction is deliberately absent, and this record is where it used to sit. The vocabulary entry in spec/enums.json sources that code from lookup_recipient; lookup_recipient answers about a mailbox rather than about one report, l.vashti@pellgrave.example is the recipient of seven emails in this corpus and reported six of them without touching anything, and no header, tool result or data file records what she did before she reported this one. Scoring a student on it would score a fact no artifact carries, so the code is gone from the indicator list and from required_indicators. Escalates once, under partner_account_compromise, because dmarc passed and the reputation is known_good, so the mail genuinely came off the customer's server and the account behind it is in someone else's hands. Blocking the host protects Pellgrave and leaves Hollinvale sending this to everyone else on Renata's contact list, so the SOC telephones them on the number it already holds rather than replying to the mailbox. Story context: 018 taught the agent to call check_urls on a trusted sender; this is where that habit runs out and the pattern has to carry the verdict. Deliberate omissions, matching the indicator list: no Reply-To, no X-Priority, no Auto-Submitted, no X-Originating-IP, no List headers, no attachment and no quoted text.

check_sender_reputation.notes: Reported by b.onwuka on 2026-03-31 (CEO impersonation); lanternmail.example is a free webmail provider and its domain reputation stays neutral.

emails.reference_summary: This is the same gift-card scam you reported in March, from the same webmail address using Adaeze's name. Do not buy anything, and thank you for catching it again.
emails.notes: Gift card business email compromise, the week 7 batch case where one tool call settles it. Key facts: the display name Adaeze Whitcombe is the company's real Chief Executive Officer, whose address is a.whitcombe@pellgrave.example, while the From address is adaeze.whitcombe.office@lanternmail.example on a free webmail provider; no Reply-To; SPF, DKIM and DMARC all pass for lanternmail.example, which publishes a quarantine policy, and that pass proves only that the mail really came from that provider; X-Originating-IP [203.0.113.88] is the webmail user's client address and is the same address 009 carries, which is what ties the two messages to one operator; the message arrived through the gateway (X-Sentrywick-External: yes) with a clean scan and a spam score of 3.9; there is no link, no removed attachment and no In-Reply-To. Difficulty medium by the tier rule: two decisive facts (sender:display_name_matches_employee and sender:known_bad) against one pressure point (no link and no attachment, so check_urls has nothing to check), which is decisive over pressure without a tie, and neither adjustment applies because there is no injection and the body-only read already lands on malicious. Playbook rules that decide the case: rule 2, an employee's name over an address outside pellgrave.example is impersonation until a phone call proves otherwise, and rule 6, executives do not ask for gift cards, wire transfers or secrecy by email. This message asks for two of the three. Body signals: the ask is eight gift cards on the assistant's own card with a reimbursement promised later, the codes are to be scratched and photographed, which is the money itself rather than an errand, the matter is to stay between the two of them as a surprise, and the sender rules out the telephone for the day. The close is a first name with no title and no extension, because a telephone number in the signature would hand the assistant the one move that ends the attack. No client, vendor or project is named in the body, so nothing in it resolves to a domain, an address or a link, and the loop is left with the sender and nothing else. Tools: check_sender_reputation matches at address level and returns known_bad, first seen 2026-03-31, one prior report, last verdict malicious, campaign tag ceo-impersonation, so the loop stops on decisive_malicious after one call; the provider domain lanternmail.example would have returned neutral, and the address record overriding the domain record is the lesson this file carries. lookup_recipient would show Beatrix Onwuka is the Executive Assistant to the CEO with the executive flag, four reports and three true positives in 90 days, and check_urls has nothing to look up, but neither is needed once the sender comes back known_bad. recipient:prior_similar_report follows the prior_similar_report_rule: content:gift_card_request implies ceo-impersonation and cfo-impersonation, the sender record's ceo-impersonation tag is added, and the mailbox holds a ceo-impersonation report, so that is the value. Expected action: escalate_incident with reasons financial_or_endpoint_impact, because a malicious BEC always escalates, and executive_target, because Beatrix carries the executive flag. She reported the message before acting on it, so user_interacted does not apply. The correct close is to confirm with Adaeze's office by telephone, block the address, and tell Beatrix that nothing should be purchased.

emails.subject: Need a favor before my 9:00

check_sender_reputation.notes: The organization's own domain. A From address on this domain arriving through the external gateway is a forgery unless quarantined and released.

emails.reference_summary: This came from Adaeze's real account, but it was sent through our webmail from an outside network at 5:40 AM and asks for gift cards, which she never does by email. We believe her account has been broken into; do not buy anything, and we are locking the account now.
emails.notes: The batch set's account-takeover case, and the hardest false negative in the corpus: every sender fact an agent normally leans on is genuine. Key facts a correct extractor produces: from_domain pellgrave.example, the organization itself; the address a.whitcombe@pellgrave.example really is the Chief Executive Officer's, so display_name_mismatch is false and sender:display_name_matches_employee does not apply; no Reply-To; spf, dkim, dmarc and dmarc_policy all null, because the message never crossed the border gateway and carries no Authentication-Results header; X-Sentrywick-External is absent, which the extractor records as header:external_flag with the value no, and the submission host still wrote X-Sentrywick-Scan-Result: clean on its own traffic; url_hosts empty; no removed-attachment header; no In-Reply-To. Received chain, three hops rather than the two an internal message normally has: the client [203.0.113.201] submitted with ESMTPSA to webaccess.pellgrave.example at 05:40:02 -0500, webaccess handed the message to mail.pellgrave.example [10.20.4.25] at 05:40:05, and mailstore-01.pellgrave.example took it by LMTP at 05:40:07; Date is 05:40:00. mailstore-01 is the store data/recipients.json gives b.onwuka@pellgrave.example, the same store 007, 009 and 029 deliver to, because a mailbox lives on one store whatever path a message took. X-Originating-IP repeats the client address. That address is the whole case: 203.0.113.0/24 is a documentation block and not the corporate network, while every other internal message in the corpus submits from 10.20.30.0/24 or 10.20.31.0/24 through mail.pellgrave.example. Somebody outside signed in to the CEO's mailbox and sent as her, which is what header:webmail_submission_external_ip names. Body: multipart/alternative with a text/plain part then a text/html part, both 7bit and carrying the same words, so a part-to-part diff is empty; the HTML part is plain paragraphs with no link, image, script or hidden text. Body phrases the extractor keys on, present whole on one line in both parts: 'gift cards' (gift card request), 'this morning' (urgency) and 'don't mention' (secrecy). The wording carries no other phrase from any list in spec/enums.json, so no payment, credential, data or channel code belongs here. The message names no customer and no vendor: the client is 'the client team we are hosting', a phrase with no domain, no address and no reputation record behind it, so the body hands the loop nothing further to look up. The signature is the CEO's own two-line block, Adaeze Whitcombe then Chief Executive Officer, Pellgrave Mechanical Group, ext. 4101, the same house shape 011 and 019 carry; an attacker inside the mailbox inherits it, so the signature proves nothing, and extension 4101 is how the case actually closes. Difficulty reason: the tier rule counts one decisive fact (the webmail submission from an external address) against two pressure facts (the From domain is the organization on the internal path, and there is neither a link nor an attachment, so check_urls has nothing to check), so pressure exceeds decisive and the base tier is hard; there is no injection, and the body-only read is uncertain rather than benign, so no adjustment applies. Playbook rules that decide the case: rule 6, executives do not ask for gift cards, wire transfers or secrecy by email, and this message asks for two of the three; rule 11, internal mail carries no authentication results and a missing check is not a failed check, which is the rule that stops an agent from reaching the right verdict for the wrong reason. For the instructor: this is the file where a header-only reader and a body-only reader both fail. The headers say internal, the address is genuine and reputation returns status internal, so an agent that stops at the sender says benign; the body is a plausible note from a traveling executive, so a reader without the Received chain is left uncertain. The two facts that settle it are the submission hop with X-Originating-IP and the gift-card ask, and a student who names both has the whole answer. Tools: check_sender_reputation matches at domain level and returns status internal, which is a fact about the domain and not a clearance for the message; lookup_recipient shows Beatrix Onwuka is the executive assistant to the CEO, carrying the executive flag, with four reports and three true positives in 90 days and three of those tagged ceo-impersonation; check_urls has nothing to look up, so the loop stops on tools_exhausted after two calls. That is why the stop reason is not internal_sender: an internal result closes 011, where nothing is being asked for, and closes nothing here. recipient:prior_similar_report follows the prior_similar_report_rule: content:gift_card_request implies ceo-impersonation and cfo-impersonation, the sender record carries no campaign tag of its own, and the mailbox holds three ceo-impersonation reports, so the value is ceo-impersonation; her marketing report does not match. Expected action: escalate_incident with reasons financial_or_endpoint_impact (a malicious BEC always escalates), executive_target (the recipient carries the executive flag) and internal_account_compromise (the webmail submission from outside). Beatrix reported the message before buying anything, so user_interacted does not apply. The correct close is to buy nothing, reach the CEO on extension 4101 rather than by replying, lock the mailbox and pull the webmail sign-in history for 203.0.113.201. Story context: 009 is the impostor's pretext from a webmail lookalike address on 20 April and 029 is its gift-card follow-through on 22 April, both to this same mailbox and both reported; this message arrives the morning after, from inside the real account, which is how the campaign escalates when a lookalike address stops working.

emails.reference_summary: This invoice comes from a look-alike of Slatemoor's domain and asks us to send money to a new bank account, which is the classic sign of invoice fraud. Do not pay it; accounts payable will confirm with Slatemoor by phone.
emails.notes: Key facts a correct extractor produces: from_domain slatemoor-supply.example, which is slatemoorsupply.example with a hyphen inserted into the supplier's name, so the From domain is a look-alike of a domain the corpus knows; display name 'Slatemoor Industrial Supply AR', which normalizes onto the data/display_names.json entry 'Slatemoor Industrial Supply', a vendor whose owner_domains list holds only slatemoorsupply.example, so the display-name check reports sender:display_name_claims_vendor; no Reply-To, so there is no reply mismatch to find and the From address is the only sender fact; spf=pass on slatemoor-supply.example, dkim=pass with d=slatemoor-supply.example s=k1, dmarc=pass with policy.dmarc=none, all three honest, because the attacker owns the domain he sends from and data/domain_policy.json shows it publishing mx -all and a p=none record; Subject is an RFC 2047 encoded word, written as two adjacent words because one would exceed the 75-character cap, decoding to 'Factura nº 44170-118 y nuevos datos ACH / Invoice 44170-118'; no link in either part; one removed-attachment header, Factura_44170-118.pdf, 61,440 bytes, action quarantined, reason archived-to-vault; no In-Reply-To, so the message opens a thread. Received chain: webmail.slatemoor-supply.example [192.0.2.165] submitted with ESMTPSA to mail.slatemoor-supply.example at 20:33:03 +0000, which handed off with ESMTPS and TLS1_3 to mx.pellgrave.example [10.20.4.10] at 15:33:06 -0500, delivered by LMTP to mailstore-01.pellgrave.example at 15:33:08 -0500; Date is 15:33:00 -0500, the same instant as 20:33:00 +0000 in the Message-ID, whose host is the front end that composed the message. mailstore-01 is the store data/recipients.json gives ap@pellgrave.example, the same store 005 and 016 delivered to, because a mailbox lives on one store whatever path a message took. X-Sentrywick-External is yes, scan result clean, spam score 3.2. Body phrases the extractor keys on, present in both parts: 'nueva cuenta', 'new ACH', 'new bank', 'new routing' and 'new account number', all content:payment_change_request, plus a Spanish half that carries the whole ask before the English one repeats it, which is content:non_english_body. No other content code applies, and the wording is held clear of every other phrase list on purpose: 'invoice' is a content:payment_request phrase, so the Spanish says 'factura' and the English says 'bill', and 'today' is a content:urgency_keywords phrase, so the Spanish 'hoy' stands alone and the English says 'Effective with this message'. The subject still reads 'Invoice 44170-118', because the phrase pass reads the decoded body parts and not the header. Difficulty reason: the tier rule counts two decisive facts (sender:lookalike_domain and sender:display_name_claims_vendor) against no pressure fact, so the base tier is easy; the body-only read is uncertain rather than opposed to the verdict, so no step is added, and there is no injection. For the instructor: this is the easy vendor fraud case in the week 7 batch, and it is the pair to 016. Both move the same account to a new bank. 016 does it from inside the supplier's real mailbox, where the only header tell is a Reply-To; this one does it from a domain that merely looks like the supplier's, where the tell is the From domain itself and a reader who compares it with the address on any earlier Slatemoor message has the answer. Three authentication passes appear on both, which is why they belong together: authentication proved the domain in each case and proved nothing about the company. The bilingual body is texture and not a tell, because the supplier's real accounts receivable team writes bilingual mail too, and the archived PDF is normal gateway document policy. Tools: check_sender_reputation returns unknown for slatemoor-supply.example, first seen 2026-04-22, one message in 90 days, no prior reports and new_domain true, so the domain is six days old at the corpus clock; check_urls has nothing to look up because there is no link; lookup_recipient shows ap@ is a shared mailbox that handles payments with three prior reports, all true positives, two of them tagged vendor-invoice-fraud. The loop therefore runs check_sender_reputation and lookup_recipient and stops on tools_exhausted. recipient:prior_similar_report follows the prior_similar_report_rule: the payment change ask implies vendor-invoice-fraud and direct-deposit-change, the mailbox holds vendor-invoice-fraud, so that is the value. Full credit on the indicators criterion needs sender:lookalike_domain and content:payment_change_request. Expected action: escalate_incident under financial_or_endpoint_impact, because a new bank account aimed at an accounts payable mailbox is money about to leave. partner_account_compromise does not apply here and does on 016: nothing of Slatemoor's is broken, and the telephone call the playbook asks for goes to the number already on file rather than to the 555-0182 in this signature. Story context: 005 is the real collections notice on account 44170, AP's reply of 14 April is in known_threads.json, 016 hijacks that thread from inside the supplier, 019 is the CFO asking to move the same payment, and this message attacks the same account from outside. Grading note: a student who closes this benign because the authentication passes has read the verdict line and not the address, and a student who calls it malicious without naming the From domain or the display name has guessed.

emails.notes: The batch set's easy malware delivery case. A one-line invoice email spoofs Cindermill Signs, a small sign company the organization has never dealt with, and carries a file named Invoice_88213.pdf.exe, a program file dressed as a PDF. The gateway stripped it for a blocked extension and left the filename, size and digest in X-Sentrywick-Removed-Attachment, so the .eml holds only text; this is the sample chosen to prove that the stripped-attachment convention downloads cleanly. Sentrywick Gateway], and close with the gateway's removal notice naming Invoice_88213.pdf.exe (184,320 bytes); both parts are quoted-printable because the banner snippet and the first notice line each run past 78 characters in source. Playbook rule 8 decides the case: a file removed for a blocked extension is malicious. Difficulty easy: one decisive malicious fact (attachment:blocked_extension), no pressure toward benign, no injection, and the body alone already reads as an unsolicited invoice with a double-extension attachment. emails.reference_summary: This is Casimir's real weekend schedule for the warehouse team, sent from inside the company, with a link to the payroll portal we all use. Nothing is wrong with it.
emails.notes: Key facts a correct extractor produces: from_domain pellgrave.example, the organization's own domain, arriving on the internal path; display_name_mismatch false, because data/display_names.json owns the name Casimir Hallowden to pellgrave.example and sources it from recipients.json:c.hallowden@pellgrave.example; reply_to_domain none, since the file carries no Reply-To; spf, dkim, dmarc and dmarc_policy all null, because the message never crossed the border gateway and the file carries no Authentication-Results header at all, which is auth:not_evaluated_internal and not a failure of anything; Return-Path is the From mailbox, because a person writing to a list from his own workstation has no reason to aim the bounces anywhere else; one link host, my.fenwrightpay.example, carrying the single link https://my.fenwrightpay.example/timesheets, which appears once in the plain part and once in the HTML part where the href and the visible text are the same address; no removed-attachment header; no In-Reply-To and no References, so the thread is new. Received chain: PMG-WS-2451.corp.pellgrave.example [10.20.31.140], Casimir's workstation, submitted with ESMTPSA to mail.pellgrave.example [10.20.4.25] at 16:20:01 -0500, and mail.pellgrave.example delivered by LMTP to mailstore-01.pellgrave.example at 16:20:02; Date is 16:20:00 -0500, the same instant as the 20260423212000 stamp in the Message-ID. The list expanded at the submission host, so this file is the copy delivered to the reporter's own mailbox: the LMTP hop reads for <h.quintanilla@pellgrave.example> and names mailstore-01, the store data/recipients.json gives that mailbox, while To stays warehouse-staff@pellgrave.example, which is what recipient:distribution_list and the lookup_recipient expectation key on. recipients.json records mailstore-02 for the list itself, but the copy the corpus keeps is the one delivered to an individual member, so the hop names the reporter's own store; every mailbox in the corpus lives on exactly one store whatever path a message took. X-Sentrywick-External is absent, which the extractor records as header:external_flag with the value no, and neither body part carries the gateway banner, because the gateway inserts it only into the mail it stamps as external. The gateway still wrote X-Sentrywick-Scan-Result: clean on its own submission, and X-Sentrywick-Reported-By names Hollis Quintanilla, who reported it; there is no spam score, which the gateway writes on external mail only. The Subject is an RFC 2047 encoded word, '=?UTF-8?Q?Horario_de_turnos_de_fin_de_semana=2C_25_y_26_de_abril?=', which decodes to 'Horario de turnos de fin de semana, 25 y 26 de abril'. It is extraction practice and not a signal of anything: the decoded line is ASCII, so the encoding is the composer's habit, this client encoding the whole Subject whenever the body it is about to send is not ASCII, and it Q-encodes the comma with it. Body: multipart/alternative, a text/plain part then a text/html part, both quoted-printable because the Spanish is not ASCII and the file has to stay seven-bit clean, both carrying the same words, and the HTML part is plain paragraphs with one anchor and no image, script, form, styling trick or hidden text. Content: the warehouse supervisor sends the weekend shift schedule for Saturday 25 and Sunday 26 April, says the split is the same as last week except that Teodoro moves from Saturday to Sunday because the forklift inspection is Saturday morning, lists each shift with its dock or the receiving desk, its start and end time and the one or two people on it, notes that the Slatemoor truck arrives Saturday around 09:00 with fourteen pallets so dock 2 stays clear until it is unloaded, asks anyone who cannot work a shift to say so by Friday, and closes with the standing reminder to record hours in the payroll portal before Tuesday noon over the one link. He signs with his first name over his role and extension 4215. Every crew name in the schedule is invented for this file and none of them is a mailbox in recipients.json, which holds mailbox owners rather than a ninety person warehouse crew. content:non_english_body is the only content code: the message is Spanish end to end, which is how this supervisor has always written to this list, and no phrase from any other list in spec/enums.json appears in either part. In particular the timesheet cutoff is named by its day and its hour and never counted down, so nothing from content:urgency_keywords fires; the portal is where hours go and never a place to sign in, so nothing from content:credential_request fires; and the extension in the signature is a signature line rather than an offer to confirm anything by telephone, so content:phone_verification_offered does not fire and no phrase from its list appears. Difficulty reason: the tier rule counts one decisive benign fact, the organization's own domain on the internal path, against no pressure fact, so the base tier is easy; the body-only read is benign, the same as the verdict, so no adjustment applies, and there is no injection. Week 7 loop: check_sender_reputation returns status internal at domain level for pellgrave.example, which is the stated stop condition, so the loop stops after one call with stop_reason internal_sender; check_urls would only confirm that my.fenwrightpay.example is allowlisted, and lookup_recipient would only confirm that warehouse-staff@pellgrave.example is a distribution list with no report history of its own. Escalation: none. The verdict is benign, the category is legit_internal, and no benign escalation rule fits, since nothing here fails authentication on a trusted sender, touches a banking item or asks an unknown sender's question, so recommended_action is close_benign_reply_to_reporter. For the instructor: this is the batch pair to 002 in the teaching set. Both are ordinary internal housekeeping that a triage agent has to close; 002 links to the company's own status page and this one links off the company network to a vendor host that the SOC trusts anyway, which is the second thing an agent has to learn to read. Grading note: a model that calls this suspicious because the body is not in English has scored a language as a signal, and a model that calls the external link a tell has not run check_urls or has not read what allowlisted means. Story context: Hollis Quintanilla reported it, which is why the file exists at all; he is the service manager and he sits on the warehouse list because his technicians pick up parts at the dock, and his record shows two prior reports, one of them a true positive, so he is not a chronic reporter and the queue takes his reports seriously.

emails.reference_summary: This is a job application for the posting HR opened this month, sent from a personal email address with a link to the applicant's own portfolio site. It asks for nothing and is safe to handle as a normal application.
emails.notes: The batch set's benign application from a stranger, and the case that shows a free webmail address and an unknown link host are two ordinary facts about private people rather than two findings. Key facts: the From address oona.adebayo.ferris@lanternmail.example is a free webmail account, and display_names.json records Oona Adebayo-Ferris as an individual who owns both lanternmail.example and oona-adebayo-ferris.example, because a private person has no company domain to write from; there is no Reply-To; SPF, DKIM and DMARC all pass for lanternmail.example, which publishes a quarantine policy, and the pass proves only that the provider really sent the message; X-Originating-IP [203.0.113.140] is the composing browser's address and X-Mailer is Lanternmail Web; the message arrived through the gateway (X-Sentrywick-External: yes) with a clean scan and a spam score of 3.5; the one link is https://oona-adebayo-ferris.example/work, a path with no sign-in on a host that is on neither list; there is no removed attachment and no In-Reply-To; the recipient is the shared HR mailbox and the reporter is Tobias Nkemelu, the coordinator who works it. Difficulty hard by the tier rule: a benign record scores a decisive fact only from the derived combinations in section 5.2, and none of them is present, so decisive is 0 and the base tier is hard; there is no injection and the body only read agrees with the verdict, so neither adjustment applies. The body only read is benign because the prose is an ordinary job application: it names the posting, describes four years of dispatch work at Thornbeck Plumbing, links her own work samples, offers references on request and asks for nothing. Playbook rules 1 and 7 both apply and neither settles it: three passes name a domain and not a person, and a host on neither list is unknown rather than clean. Tools: check_sender_reputation matches at domain level, because oona.adebayo.ferris@lanternmail.example has no address record of its own, and returns neutral for the provider with nine prior reports, the last one malicious and tagged ceo-impersonation, which is history about the provider and not about this sender; check_urls returns unlisted for oona-adebayo-ferris.example; lookup_recipient shows the Human Resources shared mailbox with one prior report, no true positives, no executive or payments flag. Every tool answers and none of them is decisive, so the loop runs all three and ends on tools_exhausted, which is the shape week 5 teaches and week 7 has to reproduce without a teaching page in front of it. recipient:prior_similar_report is absent under the prior_similar_report_rule: the message carries no ask code, the sender record's campaign tag ceo-impersonation is in sender_campaign_tags, but the HR mailbox holds only a benefits-notice report, so no tag matches. Nothing escalates: the verdict is benign, the category is not spam, DMARC did not fail on a trusted sender, there is no payment or banking ask, and the reputation status is neutral rather than unknown, so unknown_sender_asks_for_data does not apply and would not apply anyway, since the message asks for no data. Expected action: close_benign_reply_to_reporter, and the reply to Tobias is that it is a real application and belongs in the hiring folder. The near neighbour worth naming for instructors is 009 and 029, the CEO impersonation pair on the same provider: same neutral domain record, same three passes, and the difference is entirely in who the display name claims to be. Deliberate omissions, matching the manifest indicator list: no Reply-To, no Auto-Submitted, no X-Priority, no list header, no removed attachment header, and no content indicator, so the rendered body carries no phrase from any list in spec/enums.json.
